title: Reward Learning through Ranking Mean Squared Error
claim: Ordinal ratings can be used directly as regression targets by soft-ranking predicted returns and minimizing the squared error against them.
layout: Single panel, top-to-bottom then looping back; dashed backprop arrow, MSE loss at bottom-left
description: A flowchart on a white background. At the top, a row of boxes D0 < D1 < ... < D_{n-1} shows ordered rating classes. A brace beneath them is labeled 'Sample one trajectory per class: (τ_i, c_i) ∈ D_k'. Below that, a split box pairs an orange 'Ratings' cell with a white 'Trajectories' cell. Trajectories flow down the right side through three boxes: 'Forward Pass: r̂_θ', 'Predicted Returns', and a hot-pink 'Soft Rank'. The Ratings cell sends a long diagonal arrow to a rounded box at bottom-left, 'MSE(R̂(τ_i), c_i)', where the soft rank is colored pink and the rating c_i is colored orange. Soft Rank also feeds into this box. A dashed 'Backprop' arrow runs from the loss back up to the forward pass. The eye goes first to the colored Ratings and Soft Rank boxes.
caption: Illustration of the R4 training process: Given a dataset of trajectory–rating pairs, we compute the predicted return for each trajectory under $\rlearn$ and apply a differentiable sorting algorithm to obtain soft ranks, $\Rset$. Then, we minimize the MSE between the soft ranks and the human ratings.
abstract: Reward design remains a significant bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning (RL) to real-world problems. A popular alternative is reward learning, where reward functions are inferred from human feedback rather than manually specified. Recent work has proposed learning reward functions from human ratings rather than traditional binary preferences, enabling richer and potentially less cognitively demanding supervision. Building on this paradigm, we introduce a new rating-based RL method, Ranked Return Regression for RL (R4). At its core, R4 uses a novel ranking mean squared error loss that learns from a dataset of trajectory-rating pairs, treating the human-provided discrete ratings (e.g., bad, neutral, good) as ordinal targets. Unlike prior rating-based approaches, R4 offers formal guarantees: its solution set is provably minimal and complete under mild assumptions. Empirically, using both human-provided and simulated ratings, we demonstrate that R4 consistently matches or outperforms existing rating and preference-based RL methods on robotic benchmarks from OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. Code released at https://github.com/IRLL/R4.
